title: Ivan the Terrible and His Son Ivan
source: State Tretyakov Gallery, Moscow (public domain: Repin died in 1930). Wikimedia Commons, PD-Art.
caption: A tsar kills his own son in a fit of rage. Then this painting was attacked twice, 105 years apart. #art #arthistory #painting #history #oilpainting
_verify: VERIFIED 2026-10-10 (Art in Context; Harper's, May 2019): painted 1883-85, 199.5 x 254 cm, bought by Pavel Tretyakov 1885; Ivan IV struck his son with his staff in November 1581 after a quarrel over the son's pregnant wife, the son died days later; Alexander III banned the painting (April-July 1885); 1913: Abram Balashov struck it three times with a knife, shouting about blood; the curator threw himself under a train afterwards; 25 May 2018: Igor Podporin hit it with a metal pole, broke the glass and damaged the canvas, sentenced to 2.5 years.
Balashov's exact words: Harper's gives 'Blood! Why the blood? Down with blood!'; the common Russian telling is 'Enough blood!'. Slide uses 'Enough blood!', check before posting.
Curator's name (Georgy Khruslov) not confirmed by the sources read; slides don't name him.
The quarrel over the pregnant wife is the traditional account; historians debate the details. Slide says 'it is said'.
Repin repainting Ivan's face after 1913: not confirmed, not used.
Focus boxes placed on the real image (Wikimedia Commons file) on 2026-10-11; check the carousel and reel frames.

CONTENT RULE: the son's head is covered in blood, so slides 4 and 5 (hand on the wound, the son's face) cannot avoid it; boxes are kept at medium distance, but the topic itself conflicts with 'no zoom on blood or wounds'. Decide with Alex before rendering.

slides.headline: A man attacked this painting with a knife, shouting 'Enough blood!'
slides.sub: Ilya Repin, Ivan the Terrible and His Son Ivan, 1885

slides.headline: Moscow, 1581
slides.text: Tsar Ivan the Terrible strikes his son in a rage. It is said they argued over the son's pregnant wife.

slides.headline: The weapon
slides.text: His iron-tipped staff lies on the floor. One blow to the head.

slides.headline: Look at his eyes
slides.text: The rage is gone. Only horror is left. He has just killed his heir.

slides.headline: Too late
slides.text: He presses his hand on the wound, trying to stop the blood. The son died days later.

slides.headline: Forgiveness
slides.text: The son's face is calm, almost forgiving. A tear runs down it.

slides.headline: Banned by the Tsar
slides.text: In 1885 Alexander III ordered it removed from exhibition. A painting of a tsar killing his son was too much.

slides.headline: 1913: the knife
slides.text: A visitor slashed it three times. The gallery's curator was so shaken he threw himself under a train.

slides.headline: 2018: again
slides.text: 105 years later a man smashed it with a metal pole. It is still in the Tretyakov Gallery.
